sections.h2: What is Lafayette County, Missouri, like?
sections.html:
Lafayette County is a western Missouri county on the eastern edge of the Kansas City region, and Lexington is the county seat. It covers 639 square miles in total, 628 of them land, and touches Jackson, Ray, Carroll, Saline, Pettis and Johnson counties.

The legislature carved it out of Cooper County on November 16, 1820 and called it Lillard County at first. In 1825 it took the name of the Marquis de La Fayette, who was visiting the United States at that time. German immigrants arrived shortly before and after the Civil War and came to make up a large share of the people in Concordia, Higginsville, Wellington, Napoleon and Lexington.

The census of 2020 found 32,984 residents. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 33,531, a gain of 1.6% from the 2020 base.

One piece of local history stands out. After the sheriff was killed in May 1919, Minnie Mae Talbott won the special election to replace him and became the first woman elected sheriff in the United States.

sections.h2: Which towns and school districts sit inside Lafayette County?
sections.html:
Lexington, Higginsville, Odessa, Concordia, Wellington, Waverly and Alma are the best known towns, with Napoleon, Corder, Dover, Mayview and Bates City among the smaller ones, and a piece of Oak Grove at the western edge. Six public school districts reach into the county, and the levy of yours is printed on the bill.

  • Lexington R-V, which runs Lexington High School
  • Lafayette County C-1 in Higginsville
  • Odessa R-VII
  • Concordia R-II
  • Santa Fe R-X in Alma
  • Wellington-Napoleon R-IX

Metropolitan Community College counts these districts in its service area, though the county lies outside its in-district taxing area.

sections.h2: How does the Census Bureau describe housing and work in Lafayette County?
sections.html:
Homes that owners occupy here have a typical value of $216,500 for 2020 to 2024, and 75.7% of households own. Household income reaches $80,612 in 2024 dollars, and 9.7% of residents live below the poverty line.

Other QuickFacts entries add color: 20.8% of residents are 65 or older, 22.5% are under 18, 87.0% of households have broadband, 91.6% of adults finished high school and 26.2% hold a bachelor's degree or more. The 2020 census counted 14,065 housing units, 8.5% of them vacant, and 30.7% of residents lived in urban areas.

sections.h2: Who are the Assessor and the Collector in Lafayette County?
sections.html:
Craig Williams is the Assessor, based in the courthouse at 1001 Main Street, Lexington. His office answers at (660) 259-6158 or assessor@lafayettecountymo.gov from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays.

Lori Fiegenbaum has been Collector since March 1, 2003. The Collector of Revenue takes in current and delinquent real and personal tax for the county and for each district that has an approved levy, then pays out the money to schools, the library, fire districts and other entities every month.

The Assessor's site hosts a free GIS map and sells an enhanced version by annual subscription. Personal property declarations can be filed online until May 1 each year.

sections.h2: How and when do I pay a Lafayette County tax statement?
sections.html:
Statements are mailed in early November and fall due on receipt. After December 31 they are delinquent. If nothing has come by Thanksgiving, call the Collector at (660) 259-6171.

A payment mailed on time needs a December 31 postmark or earlier. Later ones come back unprocessed unless the late fees are enclosed. A single check can settle all statements, and the office takes neither partial nor incorrect amounts.

  • The Collector's website
  • The mail, addressed to P.O. Box 365, Lexington, MO 64067
  • A toll-free number with the PIN printed on your statement
  • The office at 1001 Main Street, with cash, a personal check, a card or a money order

The counter opens from 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays and stays staffed at noon. Closings around Christmas and New Year's appear on the collector's home page. You can also print a tax receipt from the county site.

sections.h2: Does Lafayette County offer property tax relief to seniors?
sections.html:
Yes. The county commissioners adopted Ordinance #25-01 on April 2, 2025 under Senate Bills 190 and 756 and section 137.1050 of the Missouri statutes, and the credit covers a senior's primary residence.

The collector's page reports that the 2026 application period has ended and promises an update when the 2027 period opens. If you applied and qualified last year, you do not file again. A new applicant uses the application form on that page, and a FAQ covers renewals.

Read the FAQ before a sale to see how a change of residence affects the credit.

sections.h2: How do I contest a Lafayette County value?
sections.html:
Talk with the Assessor, then file with the county board of equalization on or before the second Monday in July. A further appeal goes to the State Tax Commission within 30 days after the date on the board's letter.

The Commission also permits payment under protest. You send the whole amount to the collector by December 31, label it as a protest, and enclose a written statement of your reasons and your idea of market value. Someone who bought less than 30 days after the county mailed the statement, or who never heard about an increase, may skip the board and go straight to the Commission.

A corporation, LLC, trust, estate or limited partnership needs an attorney to file.

sections.h2: What does Lafayette County do about delinquent real estate tax?
sections.html:
The Collector runs a delinquent tax sale in August every year. Missouri's tax sale rules fill Chapter 140 of the state statutes, and the bidder at that sale gets a certificate of purchase rather than an immediate deed.

The county's collector pages give the month and nothing more, so ask the office for this year's date, the list of parcels and the amount needed to remove yours. Ask which tax years put a parcel on the list, too.

If you sell while taxes are open, the title company can pay the balance from your proceeds at closing.

sections.h2: What do I gather before selling a Lafayette County house that owes tax?
sections.html:
Collect a current statement and a written payoff from the Collector, and confirm that both the real estate and personal property accounts are clear. The office refuses partial payment, so the payoff must cover the entire statement.

  • Open the Assessor's GIS map and compare the acreage and address with your deed.
  • Ask whether a senior credit applies and what a sale does to it.
  • Print your paid receipt from the county site.
  • Decide with the buyer how the current year will be split.

Bring the figures to the closing so the settlement statement matches the collector's numbers.

faqs.q: What is the last day to pay Lafayette County property tax without penalty?
faqs.a: December 31. The payment must carry a postmark on or before that date.

faqs.q: What phone number reaches the Lafayette County Collector?
faqs.a: Call (660) 259-6171, weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30. The mailing address is P.O. Box 365, Lexington, MO 64067.

faqs.q: Who runs the Lafayette County Assessor's office?
faqs.a: Craig Williams. The office is at 1001 Main Street in Lexington, and the phone is (660) 259-6158.

faqs.q: Will the Lafayette County Collector accept part of a bill?
faqs.a: No. Partial and incorrect payments are refused, although one check may cover all of your statements.

faqs.q: Is there a Lafayette County tax credit for older homeowners?
faqs.a: Yes, under Ordinance #25-01 for a senior's primary residence. The 2026 window has closed, and the county will announce the 2027 window on the collector's page.
